title: The Kulfi Effect: How Indian Ice Cream Is Winning Over America, One Saffron Scoop at a Time
excerpt: From Malai's masala chai scoops in Manhattan to Kesar Creamery's gulab jamun gelato in Texas, Indian-inspired ice cream brands are reshaping the American frozen dessert landscape — and making NRIs feel right at home.
body:
When Pooja Bavishi first set up a folding table at Hester Street Market in Manhattan's Lower East Side more than a decade ago, she was not sure anyone would buy ice cream flavoured with rose petals and cardamom. The daughter of Indian immigrants, she had grown up watching her mother steep saffron into warm milk and fold ginger into desserts, and she wondered whether those flavours could survive the transition from a family kitchen to an American scoop shop.

The answer, it turns out, is an emphatic yes. Bavishi's company, Malai — the Hindi word for the cream that rises to the top of slow-simmered milk — opened its first permanent Manhattan storefront in the West Village in May 2026, joining its flagship in Carroll Gardens, Brooklyn, and locations in Washington, D.C. and Philadelphia. The brand now ships nationwide.

## A Movement, Not a Moment

Malai is not alone. Across the country, a new generation of Indian-inspired ice cream makers is turning saffron, cardamom, and mango into the flavours of an American summer.

In Frisco, Texas — a fast-growing suburb in the heart of the Dallas-Fort Worth metro's Indian-American corridor — Jay Patel opened Kesar Creamery in January 2026. Named after the Hindi word for saffron, the 1,200-square-foot shop offers flavours that read like a tour of an Indian mithai counter: Gulab Jamun (cream base studded with syrup-soaked dough balls), Saffron Pistachio, and a Dubai Chocolate scooped with kadaifi and pistachios. Patel, an electrical engineer who moved from India to Dallas in 2008, grew up in a family that ran ice cream franchise stores — but wanted to create something rooted in heritage rather than formula.

"I wanted to come up with flavors that are traditional to Indian desserts and bring a unique new aspect to ice cream," Patel told CultureMap Dallas. The response has been overwhelming. "We've had visitors from all over Texas and even as far as Arkansas and Seattle," he says. Nationwide delivery is in the works.

In Portland, Oregon, a shop simply called Kulfi has earned a 4.8-star rating across nearly ninety reviews on Yelp, with regulars raving about flavours like passion fruit, ube, and mango. "Not typically one to gush," wrote one reviewer in June, "but OMG this ice cream is amazing. It rocketed into my personal top 3."

## From the Street Stall to the World Stage

The commercial momentum mirrors a cultural one. At SIGEP World, the annual international gelato and pastry trade show held in Rimini, Italy, India was named the guest country for 2026. The event's marquee gelato innovator, MEC3, debuted a "Kulfi cream" flavour — pistachio and cashew grains with aromatic saffron and cardamom — as part of its Oriental Tales line, positioning Indian frozen desserts alongside Italian gelato traditions that have dominated the industry for decades.

The recognition is significant. For years, kulfi — denser, creamier, and more aromatic than Western ice cream because it is made by slow-reducing milk rather than churning air into it — existed in America almost exclusively inside Indian restaurants, served as an afterthought alongside gulab jamun. The new wave treats it as the main event.

## Why It Matters to the Diaspora

For NRIs, these shops offer something no amount of Häagen-Dazs ever could: the specific, irreplaceable taste of home. The cardamom in Malai's Masala Chai scoop is the same cardamom that perfumed chai in your grandmother's kitchen. The mango in Kesar Creamery's kulfi stick is the same Alphonso-adjacent sweetness that marked every Indian summer.

But the new ice cream makers are doing something subtler, too. By placing Indian flavours on equal footing with cookies-and-cream and salted caramel — literally in the same display case — they are normalising a cuisine that many second-generation Indian Americans grew up feeling they had to explain. Bavishi, who won Food Network's Chopped Sweets competition, has described Malai's mission as making South Asian flavours "approachable and delicious to everyone."

## What's Next

Malai's four-shop footprint suggests a brand ready for a bigger stage. Kesar Creamery's planned nationwide delivery could bring saffron pistachio to zip codes that have never heard of falooda. And the SIGEP endorsement signals that the global dessert industry is paying attention.

The ice cream aisle, long the most conservative section of the American grocery store, may finally be ready for a saffron revolution. For millions of Indian Americans, it is about time.
